lesson.title: The Mask That Splits an Address in Two
lesson.summary: A subnet mask tells a device which bits of an IP address identify the network and which bits identify the host, turning one flat 32 bit number into two meaningful parts.
lesson.body:
Every IP address by itself is just a 32-bit number, and nothing in that number alone tells you where the network ends and the host begins. That is the job of the subnet mask. A subnet mask is also a 32-bit value, written in the same dotted-decimal form as an IP address, made up of a contiguous run of 1 bits followed by a contiguous run of 0 bits. The 1 bits mark the network (and subnet) portion of the address, and the 0 bits mark the host portion. Once you already understand what a subnet is, a logically separated segment of a larger network, the subnet mask is simply the tool that tells every device exactly where that segment's boundary sits inside the 32 bits of an address.

The mechanism is a bitwise AND. A host takes its own IP address and the subnet mask, lines them up bit for bit, and ANDs them together: wherever the mask has a 1, the corresponding address bit survives, and wherever the mask has a 0, the result is forced to 0. What remains is the network address, the shared identifier for every host on that subnet. Two hosts are on the same subnet only if ANDing their addresses with the same mask produces the same result. This is exactly how a computer decides, before sending a single packet, whether the destination is a neighbor it can reach directly on the local link or a stranger that must be handed off to a default gateway.

A concrete example makes the arithmetic real. Take the mask 255.255.255.192. In binary, 192 is 11000000, so this mask has 26 leading 1 bits total: 24 from the three full 255 octets plus 2 more from the 192, written in shorthand as a /26. That leaves 6 bits, 32 minus 26, for host addressing. Six host bits give 2 to the 6th power, or 64, total addresses in that block. Of those 64, one is reserved as the network address, all host bits 0, and one as the broadcast address, all host bits 1, leaving 62 usable addresses that can actually be assigned to devices. So a network sized with a /26 mask, such as 192.168.1.0/26, spans 192.168.1.0 through 192.168.1.63, with 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.62 available for hosts.

Historically, early IP networks used fixed classful masks tied to an address's class: Class A networks defaulted to 255.0.0.0, Class B to 255.255.0.0, and Class C to 255.255.255.0. That rigid scheme wasted enormous numbers of addresses, because an organization needing 300 hosts had to take an entire Class B block of over 65,000 addresses or awkwardly stitch together multiple Class C blocks. Subnet masks broke that rigidity by letting the boundary between network and host bits fall anywhere, not just at 8, 16, or 24 bits, which is the entire idea behind variable-length subnet masking.

Understanding the mask is the prerequisite for everything that follows in address planning. CIDR notation is just a compact way of writing the same mask information as a slash and a number. Subnetting is the deliberate act of choosing a mask to carve one network into several smaller ones. Without a firm grasp of how a mask defines the network and host split, neither of those next steps makes sense, because both are really just different ways of manipulating where that boundary line falls.
